questions.enonce_markdown:
The Religion of the Israelites would not have come to anything without the patriarchs. Justify this assertion.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, together with Jacob's twelve sons) stand at the beginning of the story of Israel in the book of Genesis. The assertion says that Israel's religion owed its existence to them. It can be justified by showing what they handed down, while recognising that Moses, the prophets and the later monarchy also shaped the faith.

**1. The call of Abraham and the covenant.** In Genesis 12 God called Abraham out of his country and promised him a land, a great nation and a blessing for all families of the earth. In Genesis 15 and 17 this promise was made a covenant, with circumcision as its sign. The idea of a people bound to one God by a covenant, which lies at the centre of Israelite religion, begins here.

**2. Faith and obedience.** Abraham trusted God (Genesis 15) and obeyed even when asked to offer Isaac (Genesis 22). Later writers held him up as the model of faith. Israel's religion is a religion of trust and obedience to God before it is a religion of rules.

**3. Worship and institutions.** The patriarchs built altars, offered sacrifices, called on the name of the LORD and gave tithes (Abraham to Melchizedek, Genesis 14). Places such as Shechem, Bethel and Beersheba became sacred places in later Israel, and circumcision became the mark of every Israelite male.

**4. Continuity of the promise.** God renewed the promises to Isaac (Genesis 26) and to Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28 and 35). The covenant was therefore not a single event but a heritage passing from generation to generation.

**5. The formation of the people.** Jacob, renamed Israel (Genesis 32), had twelve sons who became the ancestors of the twelve tribes. Joseph's career in Egypt preserved the family in a time of famine and prepared for the Exodus. Without this family there would have been no nation to rescue.

**6. The God of the fathers.** When God called Moses he introduced himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exodus 3). The Exodus and the Sinai covenant are presented as the fulfilment of a promise made to the patriarchs.

**Evaluation.** The assertion is largely valid, because the later religion rests on the patriarchal promise. It should not be pushed too far: the law given at Sinai, the temple worship and the message of the prophets added much that the patriarchs did not know.

**Conclusion.** The patriarchs supplied the covenant, the promises, the faith and the family out of which Israel and its religion grew, so Israel's religion would indeed have come to little without them.
